arxiv:2611.05227.text: Regret-based Characterization, Information Limits, and the Sample Complexity of Auditing Adaptive Policies. From Irene Aldridge. Adaptive policies may gain value by responding to what they learn, not just by choosing actions that work well on average. This work gives an exact way to separate those gains from average action effects, and shows that audits based only on immediate costs can even get the direction wrong. It also links the size of the gain to how much information the policy uses. Auditing from the policy's own feedback logs can require many rounds, and some deterministic policies cannot be audited at all.

arxiv:2611.05221.text: Efficient Equilibrium Computation in Colonel Blotto Games. From Martin Bichler and colleagues. Colonel Blotto models two players splitting budgets across battlefields, where the higher allocation wins each battlefield's value. Efficient equilibrium computation has remained unresolved in the continuous game when budgets are arbitrary and battlefield values vary. The work gives an approximation scheme that finds an equilibrium with error at most a chosen tolerance, in polynomial time and nearly linear time for fixed tolerance. When budgets and battlefield values are sufficiently balanced, it also finds exact equilibria in linear time.

arxiv:2611.04366.text: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression. From Wenxin Lin and colleagues. Complete-case regression can give a biased estimate of a treatment's average effect when some observations are missing. This work sets out checks based on causal diagrams and on how the analysis combines comparisons among the remaining cases. For effects that vary across people, it also recommends weighting those comparisons to match the population's covariates. Simulations and examples from three areas of politics show why knowing that data are missing at random is not enough to establish that the estimate is sound.

arxiv:2611.04205.text: Optimal Subsidy Design for Productive Investment across Markets. From Alexandros Pavlis. Designing investment subsidies is difficult when producers face different markets and the government has one shared budget. This work models producers' irreversible capacity choices under uncertain demand, then turns the regulator's problem into an optimization over investment thresholds. It also derives subsidy schedules that lead producers to follow those choices. Under mild conditions, an optimal schedule exists, and the investment policies it induces are unique.

arxiv:2611.04040.text: PanelGP: A Probabilistic Factor Model for Asset-Return Panels. From Andrea Ruglioni and colleagues. Forecasting stock returns and their risks is difficult when company traits and economic conditions affect returns in nonlinear ways. PanelGP uses Gaussian-process models to estimate those relationships, and produces forecasts for both expected returns and the covariance of returns. In tests on S and P 500 stocks from 1995 to 2024, nonlinear loadings ranked stocks better and improved forecast scores compared with simpler loadings. Its portfolios also had higher Sharpe ratios than those based on instrumented principal component analysis, even after trading costs, though predicted risks were too compressed.

arxiv:2611.03938.text: Experimentally Validated Digital Twins: Evaluating Workforce Training Programs in the Age of Big Data. From Raj Chetty and colleagues. Evaluating job training from observational data can be difficult because its estimates have often differed from results in randomized trials. Using tax records for American adults and machine learning models, this study predicts what participants' earnings would have been without training, then checks those estimates against results from thirty-seven trials. The estimates closely match the trial results, and their error is sixty percent lower than with older statistical methods. Earnings gains vary by place and time, but are largest when programs help people find jobs in their target sector.

arxiv:2611.05342.text: Left-Digit Bias: Theory and Empirical Evidence from a Tax Salience Experiment. From Kaushil Patel. Demand often falls sharply when a price crosses a whole-dollar mark, but standard choice models do not explain why. This work models consumers as noticing a product only when its price falls below their personal attention threshold, with groups sharing whole-dollar thresholds. In a tax experiment, the model matches observed behavior and helps identify how willingness to pay relates to those thresholds. It also shows that a weak response to tax does not necessarily mean the tax causes little welfare loss.

arxiv:2611.05092.text: Search and Verification for Strategyproof Facility Location on Metric Graphs. From Krzysztof Rogowski and colleagues. Designing strategyproof rules for placing facilities on continuous graphs is hard, especially when the goal is to keep total travel distance low. This work develops ways to search for such rules and to certify how well they perform, using finite calculations to bound the best possible approximation ratio. For a proposed randomized rule, the checks can either certify its guarantees or find locations where they fail. The methods produce certified bounds on several graphs, and the authors show that their framework includes every deterministic strategyproof rule that can locate a facility anywhere on the graph.

arxiv:2611.04859.text: Bankruptcy Rules for Strategic Agents. From Yosef Zumer and colleagues. When claims on a bankrupt estate are private, claimants may exaggerate to get a larger share, but costly proof can also discourage honest claims. This work models the costs of supporting both true and false parts of a claim and asks which allocation rules can make honest reporting worthwhile. Several familiar rules cannot ensure truthfulness under positive costs for true claims. The TAL-1 slash N rule can, and offers the widest range of legal costs for doing so.

arxiv:2611.04686.text: Designing AI-Mediated Communication in Teams. From Wichinpong Park Sinchaisri and colleagues. AI assistants can help teams share information and coordinate, but workers may have goals that conflict with one another or with the firm. This study models how firms should choose what project information to reveal and when, while workers privately know local conditions and their preferred actions. The best approach depends on how strongly workers coordinate: limited disclosure can protect honest reporting, while strong coordination can make full disclosure and factual reports more valuable. Timing information until after reports can also preserve truthful communication.

arxiv:2611.04272.text: Agreements Have a Clock: Compute Growth and the Verification of AI Restraint. From Li Gan. Frontier artificial intelligence agreements may be difficult to sustain because countries can secretly keep advancing while a pause is in effect. A model of rival countries tracks research, knowledge sharing, voluntary agreements, monitoring, and responses to cheating. It finds that cooperation is possible when the cost of monitoring is no greater than the gains from cooperating. But as computing power grows, a secret advance reaches the frozen frontier sooner, shortening the time an agreement can hold. In one example, verified joint safety research or cheaper monitoring extends that period.

arxiv:2611.04266.text: Prizes, Shared Hazard, and the Speed of Frontier AI. From Li Gan. Frontier artificial intelligence labs race for commercial leadership, even though the risks of catastrophe are shared. A calibrated model compares competing labs with a common rule limiting research, and finds that three labs complete the takeoff period in eighteen months, versus sixty-nine months under the rule. The contest, rather than shared hazard alone, explains much of the faster race, while one lab acting cautiously has little effect. Even safety audits do not slow the race in the model if labs still gain from moving faster.

arxiv:2611.04000.text: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation. From Runlin Liang and colleagues. Elliptic++ is a widely used Bitcoin forensics dataset, but its evaluation can leak information from the future, and its address-level features are not fully documented. The study reconstructs how those features are calculated and evaluates them using only information available when each address first appears. With this time-aware setup, the random forest's illicit-class F one score drops from zero point eight four six to zero point two nine one, and it no longer beats logistic regression. The released definitions and code support fairer tests of forensic models.

arxiv:2611.05188.text: Bang-Bang Correlation Sensitivity: A Local-to-Global Dichotomy for Correlation Preference. From Yi-Chun Chen and colleagues. Choices under risk can depend not only on the possible outcomes, but on how outcomes are paired across alternatives. This work shows that, in a finite outcome space, three basic assumptions make this dependence an all-or-nothing matter: indifference for one pair with a shared distribution implies indifference to correlation across all lotteries on those outcomes. When choices do depend on correlation, the assumptions lead to a representation combining comparisons of outcomes with a term that weights the lotteries' distributions. The framework also gives testable links between choices over equally distributed lotteries and correlated Allais behavior.

arxiv:2611.05110.text: Correlation Probabilistic Sophistication. From Yi-Chun Chen and colleagues. When choices under uncertainty depend on how two acts' outcomes move together, standard models based only on each act's chances may miss important preferences. Correlation probabilistic sophistication reduces comparisons to the joint distribution of the two outcomes, and the framework shows how choices can identify a unique subjective probability. With completeness and transitivity, it reduces to ordinary probabilistic sophistication; without transitivity, it supports richer correlation-based comparisons. The framework also allows sensitivity to correlation to differ across sources of uncertainty.

arxiv:2611.04643.text: Auction Design with Private Priors and Costly Learning. From Kemal Ozbek. The work asks how a seller should design an auction when bidders privately know both their likely values and the cost of learning more. It develops a framework that accounts for incentives across different priors, and shows that screening learning costs can require changing both information gathering and later allocations. For finitely many possible priors, it gives linear programs that approximate the best revenue while preserving key incentive guarantees. A two-prior example shows that efficient later allocations may reduce revenue, while tailoring learning to cost can increase it.
